docs.title: ARC Cool Buildings Standard
docs.text:
Thermal comfort and building performance in hot, and hot and humid, climates.

Draft — imported, not yet reviewed

These pages come from the ARC Technical Criteria document of 16 April 2026. They have not yet been reviewed page by page in this format, and several temperature thresholds are still being settled. Those are flagged on the pages concerned.

Browse the pages below, or ask a question.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
• Climate and weather — Building performance is normally reported against the 'current climate', but that baseline is itself moving. Performance now has to be assessed against both current and predicted future extreme weather.
  • Introduction to the ARC Cool Buildings Standard — What this guidance is, who it is for, and why ARC has developed a building performance standard for hot and hot-humid climates rather than adopting an existing one.
  • Success criteria for building modelling and performance — The ARC Cool Buildings Standard aims for all-year-round thermal comfort in hot and hot-humid climates, principally through passive design, while mitigating dangerous conditions during heatwaves.
  • The ARC framework — two Steps and three Zones — The framework has two Steps, which set the building's overall servicing strategy, and three Zones, which arrange its form and layout. Together they support incremental improvement over time.
  • The Cool Buildings Programme — The five components of ARC's programme — design strategies, the dynamic adaptive-comfort model, building science resources, prescriptive measures and exemplar buildings.
  • What influences thermal comfort — Thermal comfort depends on six factors — four environmental and two personal — plus acclimatisation, expectation and a person's thermal history. Air temperature alone predicts comfort badly.

docs.title: Patterns
docs.text:
• Designing a heat refuge — The passive measures that keep a heat refuge below its temperature limit when the power is off — orientation, shading, reflective surfaces, heat-shedding roofs, window openings and draughtproofing.
  • Step 1 and Step 2 — Step 1 is a naturally ventilated building designed so mechanical cooling can be added later without locking out passive operation. Step 2 is a fully conditioned building that can still run naturally ventilated.
  • The three-zone strategy — Zones arrange a building's form and layout around its context, wind direction and the sun's path, so that it can still operate passively when the power fails.
  • Zone 1 — mechanically cooled and ventilated — Zone 1 spaces run air conditioning efficiently and, in less harsh climates, can switch off and work naturally ventilated. Air conditioning without adequate room ventilation is strongly discouraged.
  • Zone 2 — the communal heat refuge — A room or zone large enough for all building occupants, designed to stay comfortable during heatwaves using natural ventilation and adaptive comfort measures — and to keep working during a power cut.
  • Zone 3 — transient and buffer spaces — Corridors, washrooms, stores and showers. Because people pass through rather than stay, these can run hotter than Zones 1 and 2 — and can be placed to shade the rooms behind them.

docs.title: Reference
docs.text:
• Defining and monitoring heatwaves — How the WMO, the Met Office and the IPCC define a heatwave, the threshold methods in use, who monitors them, and why coverage gaps matter for the global south.
  • Measuring thermal comfort — the temperatures — Dry bulb, wet bulb and dew point temperature explained, plus the heat index. These are the measurements the ARC comfort model and its thresholds are built on.
  • Physiological adaptation to heat — People adapt to the weather they have recently experienced. ARC prefers the running mean outdoor temperature over a monthly average, because adaptation drops off sharply after about seven days.
  • Practical advice during a heatwave — What occupants can actually do when it is dangerously hot — siestas, moving around the building, tepid showers, fans, when to open and close windows, and a solar-backed shelter.
  • R&D brief — air conditioning and ventilation for hot humid climates — ARC's technical brief for a prototype air-conditioning unit that balances cooling against dehumidification and supplies fresh air without a large energy penalty.
  • Research resources and databases — The open datasets and published research underpinning ARC's comfort model, including the ASHRAE global database of thermal comfort field measurements.
  • Success criteria — the temperature thresholds — Zone 1 and 2 spaces should stay below the comfort model's humidity-adjusted thresholds for at least 90% of the year. Separate, higher limits apply during heatwaves.
  • Temperatures in transient spaces during heatwaves — Kitchens, bathrooms and corridors are used for more than an hour a day and must not exceed human limits — 40 °C air temperature in hot dry climates, 32–34 °C wet bulb in hot humid climates.
  • The ARC comfort model — ARC uses a humidity-inclusive adaptive comfort model. More humid climates require more stringent comfort standards, because the body's ability to sweat is diminished in humid air.
  • Thermal comfort models and their inputs — The two model families — steady-state heat balance and adaptive feedback — and the four inputs that drive them: clothing, activity, humidity and air speed.

docs.title: The ARC framework — two Steps and three Zones
docs.text:
The framework has two Steps, which set the building's overall servicing strategy, and three Zones, which arrange its form and layout. Together they support incremental improvement over time.

Overview · confidence high · Imported 2026-08-29, not yet reviewed · next review 2026-11-29

Source: ARC Technical Criteria — ARC's Cool Buildings Programme — ARC Framework

Tags: framework, design-strategy, zones, steps, overview

Cited by the chatbot as arc-framework.

The framework is designed to support the ability of building occupants to manage their health and comfort via simple, robust, 'adaptive behaviour', as local climates worsen and extreme weather increases in intensity and frequency.

It focuses designers on solutions that help future-proof buildings, to allow easier, more cost-effective measures to be installed later — glazing, insulation, airtightness, mechanical cooling, ventilation and dehumidification — when required, over time.

docs.title: The two parts
docs.text:
The framework consists of two Steps and three Zones.

  1. First, designers should decide between one of two strategic Steps. This is the overall servicing strategy for the building. See Step 1 and Step 2.
  2. Next, designers should use the three Zone approach to arrange the building's form, functions and detailed layout. See the three-zone strategy.

docs.title: Why it is arranged this way
docs.text:
The Steps decide what kind of building this is going to be, eventually. The Zones decide how this particular building is laid out to get there.

Because ARC aims for both Step 1 and Step 2 buildings to be able to operate during periods of disruption — including to the electricity supply — the three-zone approach should be used to create buildings that can operate in naturally ventilated, passive mode whenever possible or necessary.

The non-negotiable part

No ARC-compliant building should be completely reliant, for the thermal safety of its occupants, on electricity-dependent mechanical systems alone — including systems using solar and battery backup.

docs.title: Climate and weather
docs.text:
Building performance is normally reported against the 'current climate', but that baseline is itself moving. Performance now has to be assessed against both current and predicted future extreme weather.

Overview · confidence high · Imported 2026-08-29, not yet reviewed · next review 2026-11-29

Source: ARC Technical Criteria — ARC Protocols for Cool Buildings — Climate and Weather

Tags: climate, heatwaves, benchmarks, overview

Cited by the chatbot as climate-and-weather.

Changes in global and regional climates, and in the frequency and intensity of extreme weather — rainfall, wind, humidity, heat and cold — are now occurring, and are increasingly affecting the performance of long-lived structures such as buildings, and their occupants.

This is because of both:

  • the gradual increase of average annual temperatures, and — significantly —
  • the increasing frequency and intensity of dangerous hot weather events such as heatwaves.

docs.title: The 'current climate' is a moving baseline
docs.text:
Building performance is typically reported relative to the 'current climate' — which is changing globally, with changes varying regionally and locally.

The current climate is defined according to measured conditions over an agreed period of time, typically 30 years. Different time periods or benchmarks are used for different purposes, and may or may not be universally used across governments and organisations.

Benchmarks are periodically updated. For example, the UK's Met Office has recently updated UK regional benchmarks for heatwaves as a result of the changing climate. Note that different regions have different benchmarks, to reflect regional variations in climate. See defining heatwaves.

docs.title: What this means for assessment
docs.text:
ARC recognises that building performance is usefully assessed relative to the 'current climate' in any particular climate zone, climate region, or even relative to the climate in a very specific locality.

Because of faster than predicted climate change, building performance now needs to be assessed relative to both current and predicted future extreme weather events — particularly extremes of heat and humidity, that is, heatwaves.

This is why the heat refuge is a required part of an ARC-compliant building, and not an optional extra.

docs.title: The ARC comfort model
docs.text:
ARC uses a humidity-inclusive adaptive comfort model. More humid climates require more stringent comfort standards, because the body's ability to sweat is diminished in humid air.

Reference · confidence high · Imported 2026-08-29, not yet reviewed · next review 2026-11-29

Source: ARC Technical Criteria — Comfort model — Meeting everyday comfort needs

Tags: comfort, model, humidity, monitoring, adaptive-comfort

Cited by the chatbot as comfort-model.

Claiming that buildings are performing to the ARC standard requires using at least 12 months of measured data for interior and exterior temperature and humidity, and entering this data into the ARC comfort model to gauge compliance with the criteria.

This exercise can be carried out for any space in the building that is being monitored. The performance of the building as a whole can be inferred from these results, but ARC encourages further monitoring and investigation of any areas where occupants report thermal discomfort — in order to help design and building teams, and the cool buildings community, learn and improve their practices.

docs.title: Use a local model where one exists
docs.text:
The comfort model used will depend on the location. With hundreds of local surveys conducted worldwide based on the adaptive comfort method, many countries have identified what is found to be comfortable for their local populations — some, such as India, incorporating it into an official standard.

Where these local survey results are available, project owners can show that their building meets localised comfort expectations.

Match the study to the context

It is important that the local study used matches the project's specific context as much as possible.

A comfort study of residents in naturally ventilated houses would not be appropriate for assessing the performance of a centrally air-conditioned office tower in a city centre. This is due to differing expectations, acclimatisation — to unconditioned versus conditioned spaces — and occupants' differing levels of control and opportunities to adapt their environment.

That same study might, however, be used to assess designs for naturally ventilated office space where occupants have desk fans and relaxed dress codes.

The ARC website provides a database of these studies.

docs.title: Where no local model exists
docs.text:
For countries where a local model is not available, ARC has developed simple success criteria to guide designers and builders.

These are based on standard comfort models, but informed by a 'designer-friendly relative-humidity-inclusive' adaptive comfort model that "significantly extends the range of acceptable indoor conditions for designing low-energy naturally conditioned buildings all over the world".

This is the approach ARC applies when assessing the performance of buildings, the aim being to present building performance consistently across ARC's Cool Buildings programme.

docs.title: The humidity-inclusive model
docs.text:
The humidity-inclusive comfort model is based on 63 studies in 13 countries with hot climate regions.

The principal benefit of the model is that it acknowledges that more humid climates require more stringent comfort standards, because the human body's ability to sweat is diminished in more humid climates. See what influences thermal comfort.

The acceptable range for comfort in the model allows projects in different locations to adopt a bespoke target based on local humidity levels. This safely widens the applicability, range and accuracy of the ARC Cool Buildings approach.

In their published research, the researchers show that the widely adopted ASHRAE method overestimates overheating by 30%.

docs.title: Air temperature or operative temperature?
docs.text:
Operative temperature — a weighted average of dry bulb air temperature and mean radiant temperature — is technically the correct metric for demonstrating building performance using this model.

Where operative temperature can be calculated, from monitoring of room radiant temperatures using black bulb thermometers, the assessment can be improved for accuracy by using it.

A further complication arises where radiant temperatures are extremely asymmetrical — for example where certain parts of a room, such as windows or areas of ceiling, are especially hot. Theoretically more sensors would be required to pick up this thermal asymmetry, and more analysis to understand the impact on occupants.

Avoiding analysis paralysis

Where sufficient data is not yet available, use air temperature as a proxy for operative temperature if necessary. Use operative temperature in preference if suitable monitoring data is available, and where possible factor in radiant asymmetry where detailed monitoring and analysis is being carried out.

docs.title: Worked example
docs.text:
The source document illustrates performance against ARC's success criteria using measured data from a 10-person communal domestic accommodation building built in Tanzania in 2023, with data from 2024–2025, courtesy of Simmonds.Mills LLP, Huda Elsherif and Archie Worthington.

Figures not yet included

The source refers to two figures at this point — the influence of relative humidity on adaptive thermal comfort, and the measured Tanzanian building data. These charts have not yet been prepared for the wiki, and the underlying research citation is recorded in the source only as "Marika et al" without a full reference.

docs.title: The Cool Buildings Programme
docs.text:
The five components of ARC's programme — design strategies, the dynamic adaptive-comfort model, building science resources, prescriptive measures and exemplar buildings.

Overview · confidence high · Imported 2026-08-29, not yet reviewed · next review 2026-11-29

Source: ARC Technical Criteria — ARC's Cool Buildings Programme — Key components

Tags: programme, overview, resources

Cited by the chatbot as cool-buildings-programme.

These five components together make up the programme described in the introduction.

docs.title: Design strategies
docs.text: A simple and flexible 2-Step, 3-Zone strategy for designing buildings and planning building-improvement pathways. See the ARC framework.

docs.title: Dynamic adaptive-comfort model
docs.text:
The interactive model acts as technical guidance and helps with target setting for effective thermal performance design and modelling.

It is a standardised, humidity-adjusted adaptive comfort model-based tool that provides key humidity-adjusted temperature thresholds for comfortable, healthy and safe conditions in building spaces. It aids investigation of building performance and provides validation of as-built performance to the ARC standard.

The standardised thresholds can be adjusted for local conditions as required, using localised comfort survey data. ARC complements this with guidance on simplified, evidence-based temperature limits for spaces within buildings. See the comfort model and success criteria.

docs.title: Building science resources
docs.text: A library of open-source research papers, and reviews of paywalled papers. Guidance and advice informed by peer-reviewed research literature, live environmental condition monitoring of buildings, and citizen-science activity and feedback. See resources.

docs.title: Prescriptive measures
docs.text:
Context-informed scenarios to help identify appropriate building fabric and mechanical cooling and ventilation measures, resulting in a growing library of useful architectural features in the form of a 'pattern book'.

This is being co-created with international experts and communities, and shared free of charge with communities.

docs.title: Exemplar buildings
docs.text: Showcased buildings, sharing real-world insight into their performance and the stories of their designers, builders and occupants.

docs.title: Success criteria for building modelling and performance
docs.text:
The ARC Cool Buildings Standard aims for all-year-round thermal comfort in hot and hot-humid climates, principally through passive design, while mitigating dangerous conditions during heatwaves.

Overview · confidence high · Imported 2026-08-29, not yet reviewed · next review 2026-11-29

Source: ARC Technical Criteria — ARC Protocols for Cool Buildings — Success criteria

Tags: standard, criteria, passive-design, overview

Cited by the chatbot as cool-buildings-standard.

ARC recognises the need for the ruggedisation of strategies and as-built solutions, in order to help build resilience into communities preparing for the social, economic and environmental challenges created by a rapidly changing climate, with limited resources.

docs.title: What the standard aims at
docs.text:
The ARC Cool Buildings Standard success criteria are focused on achieving — principally through passive design and resilient, robust features — all year-round thermal comfort in hot, and hot and humid, climates, whilst mitigating dangerous conditions during heatwaves.

Alongside this, ARC considers how to:

  • achieve good indoor air quality through practical ventilation strategies and measures
  • minimise operational and embodied energy consumption, peak power demand, capital and running costs, and lifetime carbon emissions.

docs.title: How performance is judged
docs.text:
ARC gauges building performance using the humidity-modified adaptive comfort model described in the comfort model. Environmental condition data from monitoring buildings is used to investigate whether thermal comfort has been achieved in the whole building, parts of the building, or even individual rooms — and whether designated areas can operate safely as a heat refuge during extreme heatwaves.

Results are relevant to each specific climate category, based on the Köppen–Geiger climate classification. The ARC website provides a global map of the climate regions, as well as locating useful projects and people.

The specific thresholds are set out in success criteria.

docs.title: What ARC guidance is for
docs.text:
The guidance promotes building design and specifications that result in performance more likely to be maintained over the longer term, factoring in rapidly changing climates.

It helps establish and articulate, for building owners, clearer building management, investment and improvement pathways, whilst anticipating increasingly extreme weather events including disruption to electricity supplies — focusing specifically on heat and humidity inside buildings.

ARC considers more realistic socio-economic contexts and scenarios, which for new and existing buildings tend to favour smaller, phased building investment and measures. Typically this means incremental, room-by-room improvements over time — as required, and when finances allow. The overall aim is to collaborate to develop solutions for uptake at 'pace and scale'.

This is supported by:

  • educational material promoting understanding of building science, specifically for hot, cooling-dominated climates
  • a practical 'pattern language' library, sharing co-created design solutions
  • shared exemplar projects, to inspire and inform.

See the Cool Buildings Programme for how these fit together.

docs.title: R&D brief — air conditioning and ventilation for hot humid climates
docs.text:
ARC's technical brief for a prototype air-conditioning unit that balances cooling against dehumidification and supplies fresh air without a large energy penalty.

Reference · confidence medium · Imported 2026-08-29, not yet reviewed · next review 2026-11-29

Source: ARC Technical Criteria — Appendix 3: technical R&D brief

Tags: research, air-conditioning, ventilation, dehumidification, brief

Cited by the chatbot as cooling-rd-brief.

This is a brief, not guidance

This page describes work ARC would like done. It is not a specification for equipment you can buy today, and nothing here has been built or tested.

docs.title: 1. Objective
docs.text:
Develop a prototype air-conditioning unit optimised for high-temperature, high-humidity environments such as those found in parts of Tanzania and similar regions. The system should:

  • cool indoor air effectively
  • remove excess humidity efficiently
  • introduce fresh outdoor air with minimal added energy load
  • operate reliably with minimal maintenance and energy input.

docs.title: 2. Core design challenge
docs.text:
In hot and humid climates, thermal comfort depends on both temperature reduction and moisture removal — see what influences thermal comfort.

Standard air-conditioning units often either:

  • overcool air in order to achieve dehumidification, wasting energy; or
  • fail to adequately remove humidity, leading to discomfort and mould growth.

The design must balance cooling and dehumidification efficiently. This is the same requirement placed on Zone 1 spaces.

docs.title: A. Cooling and dehumidification balance
docs.text:
• Design for independent control of temperature (sensible load) and humidity (latent load).
  • Investigate two-stage cooling systems:
    • Stage 1: moisture removal using cold coils or desiccant systems
    • Stage 2: reheat, to deliver comfortable air supply temperature.
  • Use variable-speed fans and compressors for energy-efficient modulation.

Target performance

Measure Target Indoor air temperature 26–28 °C Relative humidity 50–60% Energy use Lower than typical single-stage systems

docs.title: B. Fresh air ventilation with low energy penalty
docs.text:
Fresh air is essential for indoor air quality, but increases the cooling and dehumidification load.

Options

  1. Integrated into the AC unit — heat and moisture recovery ventilators (HMRVs), or desiccant-based intake systems.
  2. Separate systems — trickle vents, possibly with moisture control features; stand-alone energy recovery ventilators (ERVs); solar-powered extract.

Ventilation target — supply 10–20 m³/h per person of fresh air, while minimising additional cooling and moisture load.

docs.title: 4. Context and practical constraints
docs.text:
Environmental conditions

  • Outdoor air: 30–35 °C, 70–90% relative humidity
  • Power supply: intermittent or expensive
  • Maintenance: should be low-frequency and simple
  • Noise: quiet operation preferred in domestic spaces.

Materials and build

  • Corrosion-resistant components
  • Modular, repairable parts
  • Suitable for potential local assembly in East Africa.

This reflects the wider ARC principle of simple, robust, locally repairable equipment — see designing a heat refuge.

docs.title: 5. Outputs required
docs.text:
• Concept drawings and control schematics
  • Thermal and energy performance simulations
  • Bill of materials with approximate costing
  • Working prototype for field testing
  • Maintenance and installation guides suitable for non-specialist users.

docs.title: 6. Success criteria
docs.text:
• Indoor climate: 26–28 °C, 50–60% relative humidity
  • Fresh air provision: 10–20 m³/h per person
  • Energy use: at least 30% less than conventional air conditioning
  • Ease of use and maintenance
  • Robustness and reliability in local conditions.

docs.title: Designing a heat refuge
docs.text:
The passive measures that keep a heat refuge below its temperature limit when the power is off — orientation, shading, reflective surfaces, heat-shedding roofs, window openings and draughtproofing.

Pattern · confidence medium · Imported 2026-08-29, not yet reviewed · next review 2026-11-29

Source: ARC Technical Criteria — Temperatures in Heat Refuges

Tags: heat-refuge, passive-design, shading, ventilation, heatwaves, orientation

Cited by the chatbot as heat-refuge-design.

Heatwaves pose serious risks to people's health and wellbeing, and limit their daily lives at work and at home — because in order to manage a heatwave, and even to survive it, reducing heat stress becomes the sole focus.

It is therefore important to ensure that people have access to at least one space at home, at work and in community settings for practical use and refuge during heatwaves. ARC calls this the Heat Refuge.

The Heat Refuge is a cooler, sheltered space which building occupants are able to use for extended periods during heatwaves, and which stays below certain temperature limits even when mains power cuts out. It may be a single space, or a zone including several rooms. It corresponds to Zone 2.

docs.title: The requirement
docs.text:
Temperature limit

Designers and builders must ensure that during extreme heat events the Heat Refuge remains below 32–35 °C through passive (non-mechanical) design measures.

The source document gives this limit as a range. The exact figure is still being settled by ARC — see success criteria.

docs.title: Orientation
docs.text:
Minimise the amount of time direct sun heats the walls, roofs, floors and external surroundings.

Typically this involves aligning the longest and largest external faces of the building to face north and south — in hot climates the sun is higher in the sky to the north and/or south during the day — and aligning the narrow, smallest faces to face east and west, where the sun is lower in the sky and more sunlight falls on walls and windows.

Good solar orientation of a building is an extremely effective way to reduce the amount of heat from the sun getting into a building.

docs.title: Shading to walls and windows
docs.text:
• extending the roof edges to extensively shade walls and windows — and even to shade external ground areas around the building — is highly effective at keeping buildings cool
  • adding lean-to or canopy roofs against walls
  • shading the tops and sides of windows using features fixed to the walls
  • ventilated window shutters, on the outside of the window
  • ventilated shading louvres within the window opening
  • externally positioned perforated security screens (Mashrabiya).

docs.title: Reflective surfaces
docs.text:
Brilliant white — the most reflective — or paler colours help reflect the sun's heat away from the building's roof and walls.

This is particularly important where there is no ceiling in the room and occupants are exposed to the radiant heat coming off metal roof sheets. It also works well to reduce heat being radiated onto, and through, plasterboard or concrete ceilings below. Keeping ceilings cooler is important.

docs.title: Heat-shedding roofs
docs.text:
Heat builds up quickly in enclosed roof spaces. If the hot air cannot escape from the roof space, it transfers its heat to the ceiling materials, making the ceilings hotter. Heat is then radiated from the ceilings onto the occupants below.

Provide ventilation to the roof space at the eaves, allowing cooler air in, and have dedicated areas that let the hot air out of the roof towards the top — also designed to keep the rain out.

docs.title: Using window openings for air movement
docs.text:
Make sure window openings are large enough to allow a high level of air movement. Ventilated shutters, louvres or venetian blinds can be used to increase or decrease how much air passes through a window, so air movement can be controlled by the occupants.

The important thing is to avoid sizing the openings too small in the first place, and to make sure they are placed on opposing walls of the space, or at least on adjacent walls. Rooms with a single window should be avoided.

This requires windows to be placed carefully, to provide cross-ventilation — ideally openings of equal size on opposing sides of spaces, to allow the free flow of air across the space.

If the space is to be sub-divided with an internal wall, consider making the partition 'perforated' to avoid blocking air movement from the window, thereby improving cooling cross ventilation.

Lowering the window cills provides better cooling, by allowing air to pass across more of the body area of occupants standing, sitting or lying inside.

Treat ceiling openings as experimental

Creating openings in ceilings 'to let hot air rise out of the room' is not generally considered to be very effective in domestic buildings, and may allow more heat into the space than it lets out. Treat this potential passive measure as experimental at this time.

docs.title: Draughtproofed glazed windows, for when air conditioning is on
docs.text:
Inward-opening casement windows, or glazed bifold patio doors, will be needed for the operation of the Heat Refuge in two modes — natural ventilation mode and air conditioning mode.

In natural ventilation mode the casements are open, to allow for full opening of the window area for effective cross ventilation.

Fitting an insect mesh screen across the window opening is necessary for areas with mosquitoes. This typically reduces airspeed through the window by about 50% — and airspeed is the critical factor for cooling the body.

The glass areas of sliding-type glazed windows typically occupy 50% of the opening area of the window, and their insect mesh areas slow air movement by 50%. So the reduced distribution of cooling breeze across occupants' bodies when using sliding-type glazed windows needs to be considered carefully by designers and builders.

For what occupants themselves can do once a heatwave arrives, see practical advice during a heatwave.

docs.title: Services in the refuge
docs.text:
• powered fan or fans
  • lighting
  • power socket or sockets.

If an adequate mains power supply is available, this space should also be fitted with mechanical cooling — but passive measures must be favoured, to anticipate maintaining cool temperatures during power cuts.

The reason for installing air conditioning in the Heat Refuge is that in places where power cuts are anticipated, or even scheduled, occupants can pre-cool a room with the air conditioner and rely on the good design of the space to preserve that coolth for as long as possible during the power cut.

docs.title: What differs by climate
docs.text:
Hot dry climate with adequately cool nights. A well-shaded room with high thermal mass, cooled at night by natural ventilation via large openings, is important.

Hot humid climate. The room should be provided with additional wall, floor and/or ceiling insulation, to preserve the coolth.

docs.title: Why power cuts drive the design
docs.text:
Heatwaves often come with power cuts, as power grids struggle to handle the demand of people turning on their air conditioning.

In line with the need to manage this increasing risk, ARC's approach is to design for operational resilience — to safely manage interruptions to energy supplies, typically electricity supply, whilst continuing to provide thermal safety and wellbeing during power outages.

This requires simple and robust 'passive' designs for buildings. The same principle of simplicity and robustness applies to the building services equipment: for example, the use of standardised or locally made and repairable equipment and components, adequate access to local and affordable skills and services, and businesses and authorities building and maintaining suitable and reliable supply chains.

docs.title: Practical advice during a heatwave
docs.text:
What occupants can actually do when it is dangerously hot — siestas, moving around the building, tepid showers, fans, when to open and close windows, and a solar-backed shelter.

Reference · confidence medium · Imported 2026-08-29, not yet reviewed · next review 2026-11-29

Source: ARC Technical Criteria — Appendix 1: Heatwave advice

Tags: heatwaves, occupants, behaviour, ventilation, fans

Cited by the chatbot as heatwave-advice.

During a heatwave the following advice is recommended.

docs.title: Siestas
docs.text: Siestas lower your metabolic rate, and therefore you produce less heat.

docs.title: Changing location
docs.text:
Larger houses with courtyards typically have thermal diversity, which means temperatures are different in different parts of the house. Occupants can use this by moving to a cooler area of the building — for example, north-eastern rooms may be cooler during part of the day.

This is one reason the three-zone strategy matters: it builds that diversity in deliberately.

docs.title: Taking a shower
docs.text:
Taking a shower helps cool the body through evaporative cooling.

However, a study showed that this impact is temporary and goes away within 20 minutes. The water must be tepid or lukewarm — cold water causes the body to respond by constricting blood vessels, which works against cooling.

docs.title: Evaporative cooling
docs.text:
Evaporative cooling works in hot dry climates, as it increases the humidity in the air, which lowers the dry bulb temperature.

This only works where there is a difference between wet and dry bulb temperature, and the maximum performance depends on the wet bulb temperature. See measuring thermal comfort.

It is therefore not a useful measure in hot humid climates.

docs.title: Fans
docs.text:
Fans increase air speeds, which aids sweating. See thermal comfort models for the air speed discussion, and for the caution about when fans stop helping.

A key consideration is ensuring the occupant is facing the middle of the fan, as air speeds are significantly lower when the person is not directly in the airstream.

docs.title: Closing windows and curtains during the day
docs.text:
While people in hot climates are used to closing windows and heavy curtains during midday, this adaptive behaviour is not intuitive in milder climates.

Curtains limit the amount of solar gain entering the space. However, ideally you want to stop the solar gain outside the glass — see the external shading measures in designing a heat refuge.

docs.title: Opening windows overnight and in the evening
docs.text:
As temperatures cool down in the evening, it is important to open the windows to allow the thermal mass in the building to release its stored heat.

If this process does not happen, the building will be hotter the next day.

docs.title: Creating a shelter with batteries and solar panels
docs.text:
In many cases, due to power cuts, it is necessary to rely on solar panels to power one space that acts as a shelter. The panel and battery need to be connected to a socket, a light source and a fan.

This is the practical minimum version of the heat refuge.

docs.title: Defining and monitoring heatwaves
docs.text:
How the WMO, the Met Office and the IPCC define a heatwave, the threshold methods in use, who monitors them, and why coverage gaps matter for the global south.

Reference · confidence high · Imported 2026-08-29, not yet reviewed · next review 2026-11-29

Source: ARC Technical Criteria — Appendix 2: heat waves and climate change in the global south

Tags: heatwaves, definitions, monitoring, climate, reference

Cited by the chatbot as heatwave-definitions.

Which definition applies matters practically, because it determines when the heatwave thresholds in success criteria come into force rather than the everyday comfort criteria.

docs.title: Official definitions
docs.text:
World Meteorological Organization (WMO) — defines a heat wave as a period where local excess heat accumulates over a sequence of unusually hot days and nights.

UK Met Office — defines a heat wave as a period of three or more consecutive days when the daily maximum temperature exceeds a set threshold. These thresholds vary by region, to reflect differences in climate, and are updated regularly in response to rising average temperatures caused by climate change.

This provides a useful reference model for defining heat waves contextually in Tanzania, suggesting the importance of localised thresholds and climate sensitivity when setting criteria.

IPCC — describes a heat wave as a period of abnormally hot weather, often defined with reference to a relative temperature threshold, lasting from two days to months.

docs.title: Temperature thresholds
docs.text:
Heat wave definitions typically rely on high-temperature thresholds relative to local climate baselines:

  • Absolute anomaly-based — for example, exceeding the daily maximum by more than 5 °C over normal (1961–1990 baseline) for 5 days or more
  • Percentile-based — for example, daily maximum exceeding the 99th percentile of the May–September historical distribution for 3 days or more
  • Locally defined fixed values — for example, 32 °C or above for 3 days or more in specific areas
  • Country-specific figures — India and Pakistan consider plains at 40 °C or above, and mountains at 30 °C or above, for 5 days or more.

See climate and weather for why these baselines move.

docs.title: Monitoring and recording
docs.text:
National Meteorological and Hydrological Services (NMHSs) select thresholds based on local climatological baselines and maintain records.

Global organisations:

  • WMO and WHO collaborate through the Global Heat Health Information Network (GHHIN)
  • WMO issues the annual State of the Global Climate report
  • IPCC references thresholds and observational trends in its Assessment Reports
  • Countries operate formal Heat-Health Action Plans, guided by WHO and WMO.

docs.title: Why it matters for the global south
docs.text:
Regions such as East Africa, India and Pakistan face heightened risks from climate change, with heat waves becoming more frequent and severe.

Monitoring gaps remain significant, with WMO reporting that half the world's population lacks adequate access to early warning systems.

docs.title: Central coordinating body
docs.text: The World Meteorological Organization is the primary authority for defining heat waves, setting guidelines, coordinating data collection, and partnering with WHO for heat-health warning systems through GHHIN.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Aspect Key information Definition Heat wave = 2–3+ days of unusually high temperature versus local baseline Thresholds Based on anomalies (e.g. +5 °C) or percentiles (90th/99th) Monitoring NMHSs implement; WMO and WHO set global best practices Central body WMO, working via GHHIN and WHO Global south issue High vulnerability; warning systems often lacking

docs.title: Starting points
docs.text:
• WMO's heatwave page, for official definitions and resources — https://wmo.int/topics/heatwave
  • WMO–WHO Heat-Health Warning System guidance — https://ghhin.org/wp-content/uploads/WMO_WHO_Heat_Health_Guidance_2015.pdf
  • NMHS documentation, or national Heat-Health Action Plans, for region-specific thresholds.

docs.title: Introduction to the ARC Cool Buildings Standard
docs.text:
What this guidance is, who it is for, and why ARC has developed a building performance standard for hot and hot-humid climates rather than adopting an existing one.

Overview · confidence high · Imported 2026-08-29, not yet reviewed · next review 2026-11-29

Source: ARC Technical Criteria — Introduction

Tags: overview, standard, introduction

Cited by the chatbot as introduction.

This document sets out the ARC expert group's current understanding of key technical aspects of thermal comfort and wellbeing. It includes ARC's thinking on how to increase building performance resilience in the face of intermittent power supply, and of problems related to the cost and availability of key building materials and mechanical services equipment.

It outlines ARC's building performance standard for minimising occupant overheating in buildings in hot, and hot and humid, climates.

docs.title: Who it is for
docs.text:
The ARC Cool Buildings Standard is conceived as being helpful for countries in climate-vulnerable regions, where challenging socio-economic conditions do not favour easily delivering new and refurbished buildings to the Passivhaus Standard in one step.

This document should also be used as a reference by those using ARC's educational materials.

docs.title: Why a separate standard
docs.text:
It is extremely difficult to apply a practical and economically viable universal building standard across different socio-economic contexts, cultures and regions with different regional and micro-climates. Different combinations of thermal comfort factors also interact with climate change, and with social, economic and cultural factors, in complex ways.

ARC's response is a framework built around incremental improvement — the two Steps and three Zones — rather than a single pass/fail specification, judged against success criteria that favour passive design.

docs.title: A living document
docs.text:
As ARC's understanding and experience increases, this document will be updated. Please check regularly that you are referencing the latest version.

Status of this wiki

These pages were imported from the ARC Technical Criteria document and have not yet been reviewed page by page in this format. Several thresholds in the source are still under discussion and are marked as such on the pages concerned.

docs.title: Measuring thermal comfort — the temperatures
docs.text:
Dry bulb, wet bulb and dew point temperature explained, plus the heat index. These are the measurements the ARC comfort model and its thresholds are built on.

Reference · confidence high · Imported 2026-08-29, not yet reviewed · next review 2026-11-29

Source: ARC Technical Criteria — Appendix 1: measuring thermal comfort

Tags: reference, measurement, humidity, definitions

Cited by the chatbot as measuring-thermal-comfort.

docs.title: Dry bulb temperature (T<sub>db</sub>)
docs.text:
The dry bulb temperature, usually referred to as "air temperature", is the air property most commonly used. When people refer to the temperature of the air, they are normally referring to the dry bulb temperature.

It is called "dry bulb" because the air temperature is indicated by a thermometer not affected by the moisture of the air.

Dry bulb temperature can be measured using a normal thermometer freely exposed to the air but shielded from radiation and moisture. It is usually given in degrees Celsius.

The dry bulb temperature is an indicator of heat content, and is shown along the bottom axis of the psychrometric chart, or along the left side of the Mollier diagram.

docs.title: Wet bulb temperature (T<sub>wb</sub>)
docs.text:
The wet bulb temperature is the adiabatic saturation temperature.

It can be measured using a thermometer with the bulb wrapped in wet muslin. The adiabatic evaporation of water from the thermometer bulb, and the resulting cooling effect, is indicated by a wet bulb temperature lower than the dry bulb temperature.

The rate of evaporation from the wet bandage on the bulb — and so the temperature difference between dry bulb and wet bulb — depends on the humidity of the air. The evaporation from the wet muslin is reduced when air contains more water vapour.

The wet bulb temperature is always between the dry bulb temperature and the dew point. For the wet bulb there is a dynamic equilibrium between heat gained, because the wet bulb is cooler than the surrounding air, and heat lost because of evaporation.

By combining the dry bulb and wet bulb temperature in a psychrometric chart or Mollier diagram, the state of the humid air can be determined.

Wet bulb temperature is the metric ARC uses for the humid-climate limits in success criteria and transient space temperatures, because it captures the combined effect of heat and humidity on the body's ability to cool itself.

docs.title: Dew point temperature (T<sub>dp</sub>)
docs.text:
The dew point is the temperature at which water vapour starts to condense out of the air — the temperature at which air becomes completely saturated. Above this temperature the moisture stays in the air.

  • if the dew point temperature is close to the dry air temperature, the relative humidity is high
  • if the dew point is well below the dry air temperature, the relative humidity is low.

If moisture condenses on a cold bottle taken from the refrigerator, the dew point temperature of the air is above the temperature in the refrigerator.

The dew point temperature is always lower than the dry bulb temperature, and will be identical at 100% relative humidity — the air is at the saturation line. As air temperature changes, the dew point tends to remain constant unless water is added to or removed from the air.

The dew point temperature can be measured by filling a metal can with water and some ice cubes, stirring with a thermometer, and watching the outside of the can. When vapour in the air starts to condense on the outside of the can, the temperature on the thermometer is the dew point.

The dew point is given by the saturation line in the psychrometric chart.

docs.title: Heat index
docs.text:
The heat index combines air temperature and relative humidity, in shaded areas, to express hot weather as a "feels like" value.

The human body normally cools itself by evaporation of sweat. High relative humidity reduces evaporation and cooling, increasing discomfort and potential heat stress.

Use with care

The heat index is a news-channel format that may cause confusion when considered alongside ARC's adopted comfort model. ARC's thresholds are expressed in dry bulb and wet bulb temperature, not heat index.

docs.text:

  • Wikipedia — wet-bulb globe temperature
  • Wikipedia — heat index

Section not yet written

The source document contains a heading "Dangerous heat" in this appendix with no content beneath it. It has not been reproduced here.

docs.title: Physiological adaptation to heat
docs.text:
People adapt to the weather they have recently experienced. ARC prefers the running mean outdoor temperature over a monthly average, because adaptation drops off sharply after about seven days.

Reference · confidence high · Imported 2026-08-29, not yet reviewed · next review 2026-11-29

Source: ARC Technical Criteria — Comfort model — Physiological adaptation to heat

Tags: comfort, adaptive-comfort, monitoring, running-mean

Cited by the chatbot as physiological-adaptation.

People adapt to their local environment in the short term, by adjusting their behaviour and clothing to the outdoor environment they have experienced recently.

docs.title: Monthly average, or running mean?
docs.text:
Some adaptive comfort models reflect this by taking the average mean temperatures in the past month as an indicator of predicted comfort temperatures — the ASHRAE model does this.

However, studies have shown that after only 7 days, human adaptation to changes in outdoor temperatures is significantly reduced.

The running mean is a more accurate indicator. The running mean temperature is an average of the temperatures in the last week, but the model puts more emphasis on more recent days than on earlier days. This is because you are more likely to be affected by the temperatures from yesterday than from six days ago.

This is in line with the European standard method set out in EN 15251.

Which to use

Where localised survey information is available which uses both methods, the running mean figures should be used in preference. The ARC Cool Buildings toolkits build in this preference.

docs.title: What data you need
docs.text:
The tools require the user to input only the hourly outdoor temperatures and the recorded internal temperatures.

To demonstrate building performance using the comfort model it is therefore necessary to have access to measurements of both internal and outdoor humidity and temperature, inside and outside the building.

Ideally:

  • internal and external temperature measurements recorded hourly, via data loggers
  • loggers placed in permanently shaded spots
  • the external logger well shaded and also protected from rain.

docs.title: If you have no on-site data
docs.text:
Where measured data is not available, data from other sources — as local as possible — could be used. For example, publicly available airport weather data, or data from other publicly managed weather stations.

Airport data has limits

An airport is likely to have a different temperature profile from the building and its surroundings, because airports are typically located in open landscapes and may or may not be affected by the urban heat island effect.

Figure not yet included

The source document refers to a figure showing the fall-off in human adaptation after seven days. The chart, and its citation, have not yet been prepared for the wiki.

docs.title: Step 1 and Step 2
docs.text:
Step 1 is a naturally ventilated building designed so mechanical cooling can be added later without locking out passive operation. Step 2 is a fully conditioned building that can still run naturally ventilated.

Pattern · confidence high · Imported 2026-08-29, not yet reviewed · next review 2026-11-29

Source: ARC Technical Criteria — ARC's Cool Buildings Programme — Steps

Tags: framework, steps, design-strategy, retrofit

Cited by the chatbot as steps-1-and-2.

docs.title: The two Steps
docs.text:
Step 1 means constructing or refurbishing to create a naturally ventilated building that can be incrementally retrofitted over time to incorporate mechanical systems for cooling. The building operates in natural ventilation mode, but if retrofitted with mechanical systems, becomes a 'multi-mode' building over time.

Step 2 means constructing or retrofitting to create a fully mechanically conditioned, but 'multi-mode', building — that is, one that can also operate effectively in natural ventilation mode.

docs.title: What Step 1 requires
docs.text:
Step 1 requires designing and constructing a robust, physically and technologically simple building that relies for effective performance on:

  • passive design features such as appropriate building orientation; solar shading; exterior facing materials with high reflectivity; hot air-shedding from rooms and roof spaces via carefully placed openings in the building fabric; optimising cross ventilation and airspeed for enhanced cooling of occupants; providing consistent ventilation for occupants; and appropriate use of thermal mass suitable for each climate
  • relatively simple, low-carbon and affordable technologies, including energy-efficient electric fans for additional cooling of occupants
  • comprehensive insect protection measures, such as mosquito mesh screens and nets.

These measures are set out in more detail in designing a heat refuge.

docs.title: Designing Step 1 for what comes next
docs.text:
Step 1 requires a building design to have considered the most likely future improvements that people will make to that building in order to improve its performance over time. A typical example is room-by-room addition of air conditioning.

Step 1 designs should be future-proofed so as to anticipate how this may be achieved:

  • most effectively — performance
  • most cost-effectively — reducing the amount of associated building work required to make the changes
  • most energy-efficiently — to keep air-conditioning energy use, carbon emissions and running costs as low as possible
  • and also to facilitate adequate background ventilation of rooms when air conditioning is running.

The design should make it straightforward for occupants who later retrofit air conditioning to move easily between running the air conditioning efficiently and reverting to cooling the building using natural ventilation only, when conditions allow.

The test of a good Step 1 design

Future addition of air conditioning should not 'lock out' the ability to effectively operate the building in electricity-free, natural ventilation mode.

A well-designed Step 1 building provides a straightforward, practical pathway for people to make improvements over time — adding mechanical cooling, dehumidification and ventilation, solar and battery backup, as the climate changes and heatwaves become more extreme.

docs.title: Moving from Step 1 to Step 2
docs.text:
A Step 1 building can change over time into a Step 2 building — the end stage of a process that may take several years to complete.

In some cases there may be adequate budget, and a good reason, for designing and constructing the building to a Step 2 specification straight away. Examples of a Step 2 strategy include working to the ARC standard, the international Passivhaus Standard, or — with particularly careful attention to best 'cool building' practices — to the less comprehensive EDGE buildings standard.

docs.title: Success criteria — the temperature thresholds
docs.text:
Zone 1 and 2 spaces should stay below the comfort model's humidity-adjusted thresholds for at least 90% of the year. Separate, higher limits apply during heatwaves.

Reference · confidence medium · Imported 2026-08-29, not yet reviewed · next review 2026-11-29

Source: ARC Technical Criteria — Comfort model — Criteria

Tags: criteria, thresholds, comfort, heatwaves, compliance

Cited by the chatbot as success-criteria.

docs.title: Everyday conditions
docs.text:
Monitored rooms designated as Zone 1 and Zone 2 should remain below the upper range of the comfort model's humidity-adjusted temperature thresholds for at least 90% of the time — that is, these thresholds are not breached for more than 10% of the time each year.

The thresholds themselves come from the ARC comfort model, and depend on local humidity.

docs.title: During heatwave conditions
docs.text:
During heatwave conditions, Zone 1 and Zone 2 spaces may become temporarily hotter, and the following thresholds apply:

Humid climates — a maximum limit of 32 °C dry bulb air temperature, or a wet bulb temperature of 35 °C.

The heat refuge requirement is expressed in the source as remaining below 32–35 °C through passive measures.

For spaces people pass through rather than occupy, see transient space temperatures.

docs.title: Open questions on this page
docs.text:
These figures are not yet settled

The source document carries the author's own unresolved queries at exactly these points. They are reproduced here rather than removed, because these are safety thresholds and presenting them as settled would be misleading.

  • The dry bulb limit for humid climates during heatwaves is written as "32 °C (or 32–35 °C?)". The upper figure is still under discussion.
  • The heat refuge limit is likewise given as a 32–35 °C range rather than a single number.
  • Who designates a period as an 'official heatwave' is recorded in the source as an open question. This matters, because it determines which set of thresholds applies. See defining heatwaves.
  • No corresponding limit for dry climates is given in this section, although transient space temperatures gives 40 °C for hot dry climates.

Anyone relying on these numbers for a real project should confirm them with ARC first.

docs.title: What influences thermal comfort
docs.text:
Thermal comfort depends on six factors — four environmental and two personal — plus acclimatisation, expectation and a person's thermal history. Air temperature alone predicts comfort badly.

Overview · confidence high · Imported 2026-08-29, not yet reviewed · next review 2026-11-29

Source: ARC Technical Criteria — ARC Protocols for Cool Buildings — Thermal Comfort

Tags: comfort, fundamentals, humidity, overview

Cited by the chatbot as thermal-comfort-factors.

Thermal comfort is influenced by many factors.

docs.title: Factors that relate to the user
docs.text:
• clothing level
  • activity level
  • acclimatisation
  • time spent outdoors
  • expectation of the experience
  • a person's 'thermal history' with air conditioning — either adaptive comfort use, or habituation

docs.title: Factors that relate to the surrounding environment
docs.text:
• air temperature
  • radiant temperature of surfaces
  • solar radiation
  • air speed
  • humidity

Each of these is described in more detail in measuring thermal comfort and thermal comfort models.

docs.title: Why this makes a universal standard difficult
docs.text:
It is extremely difficult to apply both a practical and economically viable universal building standard across different socio-economic contexts, cultures and regions with different regional and micro-climates. Different combinations of thermal comfort factors also interact with climate change, social, economic and cultural factors in complex ways.

Whether a particular building design or feature will deliver adequate thermal comfort in a specific localised context can also be hard to reliably assess at concept, or even detailed design, stage.

docs.title: Designers are often flying blind
docs.text:
Designers and builders are often 'flying blind' because of a lack of measured building performance data — there is simply too little or no feedback for designers as to how their buildings actually perform in the real world.

Adopting 'tried and trusted' ways of building can sometimes help. However, where evidence of effective performance of existing traditional buildings and features is hard to come by, or inconclusive, traditional approaches can also risk poor performance.

This risk is increasing. Fossil fuel pollution and environmental degradation of ecosystems have led to increasing regional and localised changes in climatic conditions. Historic or modern building methods and designs that are adequately comfortable now may not be comfortable — or even safe — in the coming years.

Borrowing from historical experience may not always help in the context of a rapidly changing climate. ARC's approach must be based on evidence-based, monitored and proven solutions wherever possible. See climate and weather.

docs.title: Thermal comfort models and their inputs
docs.text:
The two model families — steady-state heat balance and adaptive feedback — and the four inputs that drive them: clothing, activity, humidity and air speed.

Reference · confidence medium · Imported 2026-08-29, not yet reviewed · next review 2026-11-29

Source: ARC Technical Criteria — Appendix 1: Thermal comfort models

Tags: reference, comfort, model, clothing, air-speed, humidity

Cited by the chatbot as thermal-comfort-models.

According to the ISO 7730 definition, thermal comfort is the "condition of mind which expresses satisfaction with the thermal environment".

There are currently two main models that most standards are built upon: the steady-state heat balance model, and the adaptive model.

docs.title: Heat balance versus feedback loop
docs.text:
The feedback-loop view says that your body changes the situation at all four levels of heat transfer — from your internal body, to skin, to the clothes you wear, and finally to the environment surrounding you. At the body level, you can shiver to produce heat, and so on.

ARC's approach is built on the adaptive model, extended to include humidity. See the ARC comfort model.

docs.title: Clothing
docs.text:
According to ASHRAE 55-2010 and BS ISO 9920, clothing level can be estimated in measurements of 'clo'.

Where people wear traditional clothes such as turbans and saris, some local studies may provide more appropriate values than the standard ensembles.

docs.title: Activity
docs.text:
How much heat you emit from the surface of your body depends on what you are doing. Heat transfers from a warmer body with higher temperature to a colder body with lower temperature.

Activity level is measured in 'met' units, which is 60 watts per square metre.

docs.title: Humidity
docs.text:
Air that is more humid makes it harder to sweat. This is why people can tolerate higher temperatures in hot dry climates.

This is the reason ARC uses a humidity-inclusive comfort model rather than a temperature-only one — see the ARC comfort model.

docs.title: Air speed
docs.text:
Higher air velocities help you sweat, by making evaporation happen faster. This is especially important in humid areas.

However, if air temperatures exceed a certain point, a fan can no longer provide a cooling effect.

Where the fan cut-off lies is an open research question

The source document records this cut-off point as unresolved, and ARC has ongoing internal work on it. As a rough guide, once air temperature exceeds skin temperature — around 32–35 °C — additional airflow adds heat to the body by convection, even though evaporative cooling continues.

That working figure has not been settled by ARC and the underlying analysis is not published. Do not treat it as guidance.

docs.title: Air and radiant temperature
docs.text:
Air temperature is the temperature of the air around you, while radiant temperature is affected by solar radiation reaching you either directly or indirectly.

The operative temperature, often used in comfort models, is a sort of average between the two. See the ARC comfort model for when ARC expects operative temperature to be used in preference to air temperature.

Tables and diagrams not yet included

The source document contains a clo table for typical clothing ensembles, and a heat-balance versus feedback-loop diagram. Neither has yet been prepared for the wiki.

docs.title: The three-zone strategy
docs.text:
Zones arrange a building's form and layout around its context, wind direction and the sun's path, so that it can still operate passively when the power fails.

Pattern · confidence high · Imported 2026-08-29, not yet reviewed · next review 2026-11-29

Source: ARC Technical Criteria — Leveraging adaptive comfort — the 3-zones strategy

Tags: framework, zones, design-strategy, passive-design

Cited by the chatbot as three-zones-strategy.

Having chosen a Step, designers should use the three-zone approach to help arrange the building's form, functions and detailed layout.

This helps decide on the best responses to:

  • its urban or rural context
  • wind directions — for cross-ventilation cooling and heat shedding
  • the sun's daily path, anticipating the intensity of solar radiation falling on different parts of the building during the days, months and year.

docs.title: Why zones, and not a single specification
docs.text:
Because ARC aims for both Step 1 and Step 2 buildings to be able to operate during periods of disruption — including to the electricity supply — the three-zone approach should be used to create buildings that can operate in naturally ventilated, passive mode whenever possible or necessary.

No ARC-compliant building should be completely reliant for the thermal safety of its occupants on electricity-dependent mechanical systems alone, including systems using solar and battery backup.

docs.title: The three zones
docs.text: Zone What it is Page Zone 1 Mechanically cooled and ventilated space Zone 1 Zone 2 Communal heat refuge, naturally ventilated Zone 2 Zone 3 Transient and buffer spaces Zone 3

docs.title: What applies to every zone
docs.text:
All zones should be secure, insect-protected, well-shaded, and able to be effectively naturally ventilated.

The building should also offer its occupants a survivable refuge from extreme heat events — see designing a heat refuge.

docs.title: Using zones to shade each other
docs.text:
Zone 3 'buffer' spaces tend to be positioned adjacent to the areas of the building most exposed to sun, where shading can be difficult or costly to achieve. East and west elevations are good examples, where low-angle sun makes shading of walls difficult.

These buffer spaces can then be used to shade the Zone 1 and Zone 2 rooms behind them.

Diagrams not yet included

The source document refers to three illustrations at this point — a notional building with only Zones 2 and 3; the same building with Zones 1, 2 and 3; and a school design in Tanzania showing Zone 3 buffer spaces on the east and west elevations. These drawings have not yet been prepared for the wiki.

docs.title: Temperatures in transient spaces during heatwaves
docs.text:
Kitchens, bathrooms and corridors are used for more than an hour a day and must not exceed human limits — 40 °C air temperature in hot dry climates, 32–34 °C wet bulb in hot humid climates.

Reference · confidence medium · Imported 2026-08-29, not yet reviewed · next review 2026-11-29

Source: ARC Technical Criteria — Temperatures of transient spaces during heatwaves

Tags: criteria, thresholds, zones, heatwaves

Cited by the chatbot as transient-space-temperatures.

These are spaces that people need to use for more than an hour each day — kitchens, bathrooms and corridors. They correspond broadly to Zone 3.

These spaces should not exceed the human limits for temperature.

docs.title: The limits
docs.text:
Climate Limit Hot dry Air temperature of 40 °C Hot humid Wet bulb temperature of 32–34 °C — the limit of human capacity

For what dry bulb and wet bulb temperature mean, see measuring thermal comfort.

docs.title: How these differ from Zone 1 and 2 limits
docs.text:
These are survivability limits, not comfort limits. They are higher than the success criteria that apply to Zone 1 and Zone 2 spaces, because occupants pass through rather than remain.

A space that meets this limit is not comfortable. It is merely not dangerous for the period someone spends in it.

Range not yet settled

The hot humid wet bulb limit is given in the source as a range, 32–34 °C, rather than a single figure. Confirm with ARC before relying on it.

docs.title: Zone 1 — mechanically cooled and ventilated
docs.text:
Zone 1 spaces run air conditioning efficiently and, in less harsh climates, can switch off and work naturally ventilated. Air conditioning without adequate room ventilation is strongly discouraged.

Pattern · confidence high · Imported 2026-08-29, not yet reviewed · next review 2026-11-29

Source: ARC Technical Criteria — Zone 1 — Mechanically cooled and ventilated

Tags: zones, cooling, ventilation, air-conditioning

Cited by the chatbot as zone-1-mechanically-cooled.

Zone 1 areas must be able to operate energy-efficiently in mechanical cooling and ventilation mode — and, for less harsh climates, to be able to turn off the mechanical systems and operate effectively in natural ventilation mode when external conditions allow.

docs.title: Balancing cooling and dehumidification
docs.text:
Dehumidification — 'latent cooling of the air' — should be optimised alongside air cooling — 'sensible cooling of the air' — if suitable equipment and controls are available.

Why this matters is explained in humidity and thermal comfort.

docs.title: Ventilating a room that is being air conditioned
docs.text:
Ventilation of rooms, for when air conditioning is running, may be:

  • a continuous mechanical extract ventilation (MEV) fan — either for individual rooms, or a larger extract fan serving several rooms — with fresh air supply to each room via trickle vents; or
  • a mechanical ventilation system supplying fresh air and extracting stale air from rooms with 'coolth' recovery (MVCR), if budget and supply chain allow.

Air conditioning without ventilation

Air conditioning without adequate room ventilation is strongly discouraged.

ARC has set out what it would like from better-suited equipment in an R&D brief for hot humid climates.

docs.title: Relationship to the other zones
docs.text:
The additional measures needed for a Zone 1 space sit on top of those already required for Zone 2 and Zone 3 spaces. The purpose is to ensure that energy use, carbon emissions and running costs are minimised.

A Zone 1 space still has to work when the power is off. See designing a heat refuge for the passive measures that make that possible.

docs.title: Zone 2 — the communal heat refuge
docs.text:
A room or zone large enough for all building occupants, designed to stay comfortable during heatwaves using natural ventilation and adaptive comfort measures — and to keep working during a power cut.

Pattern · confidence medium · Imported 2026-08-29, not yet reviewed · next review 2026-11-29

Source: ARC Technical Criteria — Zone 2

Tags: zones, heat-refuge, heatwaves, passive-design

Cited by the chatbot as zone-2-heat-refuge.

docs.title: Performance requirements
docs.text:
A communal heat refuge, designed to stay comfortable during heatwaves using natural ventilation and adaptive comfort cooling measures.

It must be large enough to accommodate all building occupants — a dedicated room or zone for use during extreme heatwaves.

This space may include some mechanical cooling. If it relies on mechanical cooling, that cooling needs to continue to operate during power cuts — so battery backup, ideally solar fed.

External planting for shading, and anything else that helps, should also be considered.

docs.title: How to design it
docs.text: The detailed passive measures — orientation, shading, reflective surfaces, heat-shedding roofs, window openings and draughtproofing — are set out in designing a heat refuge, along with the temperature limits that apply.

docs.title: Temperature criteria
docs.text:
Zone 2 spaces are subject to the same everyday comfort criteria as Zone 1: they should remain below the upper range of the comfort model's humidity-adjusted temperature thresholds for at least 90% of the time.

Separate limits apply during heatwave conditions. See success criteria.

Wording still being settled

The source document's description of Zone 2 is incomplete in one place — the phrase "designed to stay comfortable during using natural ventilation" appears to be missing a word. The substance above is faithful to the source; the exact wording needs confirming with ARC.

docs.title: Zone 3 — transient and buffer spaces
docs.text:
Corridors, washrooms, stores and showers. Because people pass through rather than stay, these can run hotter than Zones 1 and 2 — and can be placed to shade the rooms behind them.

docs.title: Performance requirements
docs.text:
A space that is naturally ventilated, using the same adaptive-comfort cooling measures as Zone 2 areas — but which, because of the transitory functions of these spaces, is able to accommodate higher temperatures than the ARC temperature limits for Zones 1 and 2.

Typical Zone 3 spaces are corridors, washrooms, storage rooms and showers.

docs.title: How they are cooled
docs.text:
Cooling comes mainly from:

  • effective cross-ventilation, or
  • heat shedding via openings in ceilings, which creates air movement,

with electric ceiling or wall fans used when extra cooling is needed.

docs.title: Where they go
docs.text:
These rooms will tend to be positioned adjacent to the areas of the building most exposed to sun, where shading can be difficult or costly to achieve. East and west elevations are good examples, where low-angle sun makes shading of walls difficult.

These 'buffer' spaces can then be used to shade other rooms — see the three-zone strategy.

docs.title: Temperature limits
docs.text:
Zone 3 spaces are still subject to a limit: they are spaces people need to use for more than an hour each day, and they should not exceed the human limits for temperature.

See transient space temperatures for the figures.
